children: Former U.S. District Judge Alan Albright, whose court in Waco, Texas, was once the most prominent venue in the United States for patent litigation, has joined international law firm A&O Shearman as an intellectual property litigation partner in Austin, the firm said on Tuesday.
Under Albright, the Waco courthouse became the busiest U.S. patent court, at one point hearing around 25% of all patent cases in the country.
Albright, 66, announced his departure from the bench in April. He had relocated from Waco to Austin last year.
The judge was a patent litigator at Bracewell LLP before being appointed to the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Texas by President Donald Trump in 2018.
Albright told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday that he "really missed the counselor side of being a lawyer," and that he was eager to join a firm with a large international presence.
"I think I could be a much better counselor now than I was before I went on the bench," Albright said.

A&O Shearman was created in 2024 by the merger of London-founded Allen & Overy and New York's Shearman & Sterling. Laetitia Benard, the firm's global head of IP Litigation, in a statement said Albright "has presided over many of the country's most significant IP and technology disputes, and his experience will be invaluable to clients navigating complex cases."

Patent owners flocked to Albright's court in ​part because of the fast pace with which he handled their cases. Critics, including Republican Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Democratic Senator Patrick Leahy of Vermont, said that Albright improperly ‌solicited patent ⁠plaintiffs to sue in his court and attracted “patent trolls” that generate revenue solely by raising infringement claims.

The senators in a 2021 letter expressed concerns about the "extreme concentration" of cases in Albright's court and the "unseemly and inappropriate conduct that has accompanied this phenomenon." That letter was directed to ​Chief U.S. Supreme Court Justice ​John Roberts, who in response pledged ⁠to direct the Judicial Conference of the United States to address how venue is chosen for patent cases.

"There was, for some reason, some public impression that I was inviting patent litigation in a way that was untoward," Albright said on Tuesday. But "if you were tracking the actual trial results," it was "as close as you're going to get statistically to a 50-50 split" between verdicts for plaintiffs and defendants, the former judge added.
He said patent litigation was "sort of self-selecting" for high-quality lawyers, which he enjoyed having in his courtroom.

The Western District of Texas' then-chief judge, Orlando Garcia, moved to break up Albright’s patent ​docket in July 2022 by issuing an order that ensured that any new patent cases ​filed in Waco ⁠would be randomly assigned.

The district's share of new U.S. patent cases was down to 11.5% in 2025, according to a report from Unified Patents, while the Eastern District of Texas was the most prominent U.S. patent court with 27.7% of patent case filings.
